history.period: Ancient; badly damaged by fire in the early 1900s; current sanctum rebuilt in traditional Kerala style
history.summary: Sree Poornathrayeesa Temple at Tripunithura (about 8 km from Ernakulam) is a major Vaishnavite temple and was the first among the eight royal temples of the Kochi kingdom, its deity being the guardian and national deity of Cochin. Legend says Arjuna obtained an idol of Vishnu from Shiva to lift a Brahmin family's infertility curse, and, guided by Ganesha to the divine Purna Veda Puri (later Tripunithura), installed it here; the deity is the rare seated Santhana Gopala Murthy under the five-hooded serpent Anantha (the folded serpent forming the throne), and the Ganesha shrine unusually faces south. The moolasthanam (original seat) is said to be at Poonithura Sree Krishna Temple 1.5 km west, from where the deity was later moved. The temple was nearly ruined by a major fire in the early 1900s and the current structure is the renovated one; the side walls of the sanctum are decorated with brass sheets of gods and goddesses and the roof with copper sheets. CSV town corrected: the temple is at Tripunithura, not Kochi proper.

name: Sri Poornathrayeesa Temple
town_description: Tripunithura (Thrippunithura) is the former capital and royal seat of the Kingdom of Cochin, now a suburb of Kochi in Ernakulam district about 8 km southeast of Ernakulam. It was the administrative centre of the Kochi Rajas, and the Hill Palace (the largest archaeological museum in Kerala) stands here. The town remains a cultural hub, famous for its temples and the Athachamayam procession that opens the Onam celebrations.
